Travelling in Egypt During Ramadan: What Changes

Is it OK to travel to Egypt in Ramadan? What stays open, what changes for restaurants and alcohol, the rhythm of the day, iftar and Eid, with 2027 dates

16 November 2026 · 12 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Sillage Égypte journey designer. Last updated: November 2026.

The quick answer

Yes, travelling in Egypt during Ramadan is entirely fine, and often quietly rewarding. The ancient sites and museums stay open, on shorter days; hotels serve guests who are not fasting; guides, drivers and boats work as normal. What changes is rhythm: gentle mornings, slow middays, and evenings (iftar, then lantern-lit streets) as the highlight. Ramadan 2027 is expected to run from about 8 February to about 9 March, with Eid al-Fitr around 9 to 10 March, subject to the moon sighting.

Key facts

Fact Detail
Ramadan 2027 Expected from about 8 February to about 9 March (29 or 30 days); the start is confirmed by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta after the moon sighting, and some calendars show a day later
Eid al-Fitr 2027 Expected around 9 to 10 March; a public holiday of several days
Sites and museums Open, on shortened days; hours are announced each year
The fast From dawn to sunset: in Cairo from roughly 5 a.m. until iftar, about 17:37 at the start of the month and about 18:03 by early March, some thirteen hours
Restaurants Many local places close by day and reopen at iftar; hotel restaurants serve guests all day
Alcohol Varies by outlet and city; check rather than assume
Evenings Iftar at sunset, then lit streets and cafés open past midnight
With Sillage Private throughout; the day is paced around the fast. Plan your journey

Every winter the same careful question reaches our journey designers: we have found dates in late February or March, so is travelling in Egypt during Ramadan a mistake? It is not. Egypt stays open and, for four weeks, keeps a different clock. This post covers what actually changes for travellers: site and museum hours, restaurants and alcohol, the shape of the day, and the evenings, which are the best of Cairo's year. It sits beside our piece on Christmas and New Year in Egypt: the festive fortnight and Ramadan are the two seasons that most re-shape the Egyptian calendar. Sillage Égypte (sillage-egypte.com), the private Egypt journey designer, plans journeys during Ramadan, and because every journey is private throughout (your own certified Egyptologist, your own car, the dahabiya chosen for your dates) the day can be re-shaped around the fast: long site mornings, rested afternoons, evenings given to the lit streets.

Is it OK to travel to Egypt during Ramadan?

Yes. Travelling in Egypt during Ramadan is welcome, and Egyptians will tell you so with some warmth. Ramadan is a working month, not a closure: the sites, museums, hotels, trains and airports all keep going, to gentler hours. Visitors are not expected to fast, and no one will check on yours; what Egyptians hope for, and repay with patience and invitations, is courtesy over food and dress, which we come to below.

The case for going is real. February and March are among Egypt's finest months: typical daytime highs in February are around 21 to 24°C in Cairo and the mid-twenties in Luxor and Aswan, warming through March (Rough Guides). The evenings are the most atmospheric of the year: the iftar meal at sunset, then Islamic Cairo strung with lanterns and busy past midnight. And it is a month of visible hospitality, warmly extended to travellers.

The honest counsel: Egypt without Ramadan is marginally easier, with full hours, full tempo, lunch anywhere and a bar whenever you want one. If you want the country at full speed, or your perfect evening is a crawl between bars, travel in April or October instead. If what draws you is Egypt as it actually lives, put Ramadan on the shortlist.

Who Ramadan travel suits, and who should go another month

Ramadan travel suits curious first-timers, slow travellers, couples and returning visitors who have seen Egypt at convention speed; families with older children who can move dinner late fit it well, though with toddlers it is harder work. It does not suit travellers who need every museum hour, every restaurant and every shop at full availability, or who would chafe at a day that rests between its two liveliest ends. For a month-by-month comparison of weather, crowds and prices, read when to go to Egypt.

What is open during Ramadan in Egypt?

Practically everything a traveller comes for stays open; the change is in the hours, not the doors. The Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announces Ramadan hours each year. The recent pattern has been earlier closing: Giza and Saqqara open until about 16:30, the Valley of the Kings 6:00 to 16:00, and Cairo museums closing in mid-afternoon. In Ramadan 2026 the Grand Egyptian Museum's exhibition halls ran from 9:00 to 16:00, with the last tickets sold at 15:00 (Egypt Telegraph). Hours for 2027 are not yet announced, so we confirm those that apply to your dates; the official monuments site publishes current hours.

What During Ramadan What it means for you
Ancient sites Open, closing earlier: around 16:00 to 16:30 in recent years Morning entries still work; nothing need be missed
Museums Open on shortened hours; the Grand Egyptian Museum's halls ran 9:00 to 16:00 in 2026 Give the Grand Egyptian Museum its morning
Hotel restaurants Serve guests through the day Hotel meals continue; room service as normal
Local restaurants and street cafés Many close through daylight, reopen at iftar and run late Book the evening; take lunch at the hotel
Alcohol Varies by outlet and city: hotel bars commonly serve non-Muslim guests, though service may be reduced or moved to one room; many standalone bars and off-licences pause for the month; Red Sea resorts run much as usual Check rather than assume; we can check your hotels for you
Shops and bazaars Open later in the morning, much later at night; Khan el-Khalili is busiest after dark Evening shopping, a midday rest
Trains, flights and drivers Run as normal; roads tighten before sunset; Eid-week services fill Book internal flights early if your dates touch Eid

The shortened hours bite hardest on Cairo's museum days. On the Nile the rhythm matters more than the clock: temples are visited early or late in the day, and the boat keeps its own timetable.

What happens to the rhythm of the day?

The day turns gently upside down. Muslims fast from fajr, the dawn prayer, to maghrib, the sunset prayer: in Cairo in February and March 2027, from roughly 5 a.m. until iftar, some thirteen hours without food, drink or water. Iftar is expected at about 17:37 at the start of the month (La Presse) and about 18:03 by early March (Wego). Prayer shapes the hours too: the five daily prayers continue, and tarawih, the extra nightly prayer of Ramadan, fills the mosques after nightfall.

The practical consequence for you is energy. Mornings are fresh; early afternoon is the low ebb, felt by drivers, guards and waiters who are fasting, never complained of, simply there, and we plan around it privately, front-loading the monuments and guarding a restful middle of the day. Just before sunset the roads jam as Egypt drives home to break the fast; we plan around that window. After iftar the cities refill and stay up late; sahoor, the last meal before dawn, runs past midnight, which is why the mornings after are among the quietest of Egypt's year.

A Ramadan day in Cairo, hour by hour

One day from late February, as we would shape it:

  • 08:00: breakfast at the hotel, served without fuss to guests who are not fasting.
  • 09:00: the Grand Egyptian Museum from its Ramadan opening; the first hour is the quiet one.
  • 13:00: back to the hotel for the long, still middle of the afternoon: rest, the pool, letters home.
  • 17:00: set out for iftar before the roads tighten, to a table we can arrange for you.
  • About 17:55: sunset and the call to break the fast; dates and water, lentil soup, then a full table while the city eats at once.
  • 20:00: El-Muizz street under its lanterns; the lanes of Khan el-Khalili; mint tea above the crowd.
  • 23:00: the city still wide awake; the sensible traveller is not.

Practical notes

  • After late sahoor nights Egypt sleeps in, so a nine-o'clock opening can feel unusually quiet.
  • Keep the roads clear between about 16:45 and sunset: Egypt is driving home to break its fast. We plan around it.
  • The odd-numbered nights of the final ten are the holiest, and the 27th night is widely held to be Laylat al-Qadr, in 2027 expected on the evening of about 5 March, subject to the moon sighting, when the mosques stay full and the streets around Al-Hussein hardly sleep.
  • Neighbourhoods lay charity tables at sunset so that no one breaks the fast alone; pass them warmly, contribute if you wish, and leave the seats to those who need them.

What is iftar, and why is the evening the highlight?

Iftar is the meal that breaks the fast at sunset: dates and water first, by tradition, then soup, then the full table. In Cairo it happens all at once: restaurants hold reservations made days ahead, hotel dining rooms lay long buffets, and family kitchens send smells down stairwells while the streets briefly empty. For a traveller it is the evening event. An iftar in Cairo, at a hotel or a restaurant, or one we can arrange on the deck of a private dahabiya moored somewhere quiet on the Nile, is one of the memorable dinners Egypt offers.

After dinner the evening continues: streets strung with lights, children carrying the fanoos, the Ramadan lantern, a Cairo tradition going back centuries, cafés running past midnight, families out walking off the meal. None of it is staged for visitors. You are simply included, and an invitation to a family table is a genuine one; accept it.

What about eating, drinking and dress during Ramadan?

Visitors may eat and drink normally through the day, and discretion is the courtesy. Eat seated, at the hotel, in the restaurants that stay open, aboard the boat, rather than while walking through fasting streets. Eating or smoking openly by day is considered disrespectful and can draw attention (Pure Nile Tours), though most visitors will simply meet patience; the gesture is noticed and returned.

Alcohol varies rather than being ruled by any single law of the month: hotel bars commonly serve non-Muslim guests, sometimes at reduced hours or in one room; many standalone bars and off-licences pause until Eid; and the Red Sea resorts run much as usual. We can check the position at each place on your journey before you travel, rather than promise a rule the month does not have.

Dress counts for more during Ramadan: shoulders and knees covered, looser cuts, most of all in Islamic Cairo, in villages and inside mosques. Within Red Sea hotel grounds, ordinary beach dress applies.

Should you plan around Eid al-Fitr?

Yes: fix the date, and treat the days that follow as a national holiday. Eid al-Fitr, the festival that ends the fast, is expected on 9 or 10 March 2027 (Egypt's Dar al-Ifta confirms the sighting of the new moon), and it runs for several days as a public holiday: offices close, kahk, the powdered-sugar Eid cookies, come out of every household, and Egyptian families travel. Trains and domestic flights fill, so book anything internal early or plan to be still. Cairo over Eid is a family city, with the parks full and Giza and the Citadel busy with Egyptian families by afternoon. The calmest place to spend the festival is on the river, where a private dahabiya keeps its own quiet. If Eid closes your journey, you leave Egypt at its most festive.

FAQ

Can tourists eat and drink during the day in Egypt in Ramadan? Yes. Visitors are not expected to fast, and hotel restaurants, room service and the restaurants that stay open serve through the day. Courtesy asks that you eat seated rather than while walking, and that you accept many local cafés staying shut until sunset.

Is alcohol available during Ramadan in Egypt? It varies by outlet and city rather than by any blanket rule. Hotel bars commonly serve non-Muslim guests during the month, sometimes with reduced service; many standalone bars and off-licences pause until Eid; Red Sea resorts run much as usual. We can check the position at each hotel on your journey before you travel.

Do Nile cruises and dahabiyas operate during Ramadan? Yes, the river keeps running. Large cruise ships sail their normal season with full board; a private dahabiya sets its own timetable, serves meals aboard as usual, and we can arrange an iftar on deck at a quiet anchorage.

Is Cairo worth visiting during Ramadan, or better after it? If evenings interest you, yes: an iftar table in Cairo, the lanterns of El-Muizz street and the late-night streets are the city at its most itself, and the sites are quieter by day. After Eid, Cairo returns to its ordinary tempo: easier logistics, plainer evenings.

What is Egypt like in the days just after Eid al-Fitr? A holiday week. Offices and many shops close, families travel, so trains and domestic flights fill and the parks are crowded; the sites stay open and busy with Egyptian families by afternoon. Museum and site hours return to their usual schedules once the holiday passes.

The takeaway

Ramadan changes Egypt's hours, not its welcome: sites open on gentler schedules, days slow at midday, and the evenings (iftar, lanterns, late streets) become the point of the day. Travellers who move with that rhythm get one of the quietest and warmest Egypts on offer.
